prs.title: feat(pool): run one model across everyone's machines
prs.body:
## What

`/pool` runs one model across everyone's machines in a group or the lobby, so a room can run a model too big for any single laptop.

```
alice> /pool give on
bob>   /pool start qwen2.5:72b
🤖 is loading qwen2.5:72b across this machine and alice (16 GB RAM), carol (32 GB RAM). This can take a few minutes.
🤖 qwen2.5:72b is ready, pooled across this machine and alice (16 GB RAM), carol (32 GB RAM). Mention @ai to ask it.
```

- `/pool give on|off`: let pools in your groups use this machine's memory. **Off by default.**
- `/pool start [MODEL]`: an Ollama model name (resolved to its GGUF blob through Ollama's manifest) or a `.gguf` path. Asks the givers in this conversation, waits up to 20 s, then starts `llama-server --rpc …` across whoever answered.
- `/pool stop`, `/pool bin FOLDER`, `/pool` (status).
- While a pool runs, the host's `@ai` answers come from it, and lending (`/ai share`) offers it as `MODEL, pooled`. `@home` tool turns stay on Ollama.

## How it works

- **Arranging a pool:** new hidden one-to-one messages (`home::pool::Wire`: `Give`/`Keep`/`Join`/`Ready`/`Refuse`/`Leave`), sent over MLS on the same path as model lending. The engine tracks givers, refuses a `Join` from anyone it doesn't share the group with, and gives home each peer's IP from its direct stream.
- **Workers:** each giver starts `ggml-rpc-server --host 127.0.0.1 --cache` (or the older `rpc-server`) and opens a tunnel listener.
- **Tunnel (`home/tunnel.rs`):** llama.cpp's RPC has no authentication or encryption, so it never crosses the network as plain RPC.
  - The host mints a 32-byte key per giver per pool and sends it inside `Join` (MLS-encrypted).
  - Each TCP connection swaps fresh nonces, then derives separate host→worker and worker→host keys with HKDF-SHA256. Frames are length-prefixed ChaCha20-Poly1305 with counter nonces.
  - Nothing reaches the worker's RPC server until a frame has decrypted, and the worker accepts connections only from the host's IP.
  - Before loading, the host probes each giver with an empty sealed frame each way, so a wrong key fails up front without touching the RPC server.
- **Lifecycle:**
  - A pool ends if any member leaves or drops off the network, or if llama-server or a giver's RPC server stops by itself.
  - llama.cpp processes are tracked in a registry and killed on `/pool stop`, on drop, and when hopchat exits.
  - Their output goes to `pool.log` in the data directory.

## Security note

A pool host can run any computation llama.cpp's RPC server allows on a giver's machine, and llama.cpp calls that server a proof of concept. That's why giving is opt-in, limited to groups you share, and announced with a note. The README says so.

## Testing

- `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` is clean, and `cargo test --locked` passes (267 passed).
- New unit tests:
  - Tunnel: bytes survive a round trip across several connections and frames; a wrong key reaches nothing; plain RPC is refused; only the host's IP may connect; dropping a listener closes its connections; frames can't be replayed across directions or connections.
  - Pool: the wire format round-trips; Ollama manifest resolution (library, user, and `hf.co` names, plus path-traversal rejection); `.gguf` paths.
- Two end-to-end tests, `a_host_and_a_giver_pool_a_model` and `stopping_while_loading_stops_llama_server`, run in CI. They skip themselves when python3 is missing.
  - Two `Home`s arrange a pool through each other's hidden messages, with Python stand-ins for `llama-server` and `ggml-rpc-server`.
  - The stand-in server only answers after echoing 200 KB through each worker's encrypted tunnel.
  - They then check that `/pool stop` makes the giver leave, and that stopping mid-load kills llama-server.
- Also covered: late givers let go when gathering ends, `/pool give off` leaving a served pool, a repeated `Join`, givers without a direct link, llama.cpp exiting after start on either side, the pooled offer and lending, `ask` errors, frame size limits, and a probe with the wrong key.

prs.title: fix: make local verdicts match what GitHub would say
prs.body:
## Why

I checked wrkflw against GitHub on wrkflw's own CI history. It was fast: emulation took 73–93 s on a Mac, where GitHub took 160–269 s. It was not trustworthy:

| Finding | Effect |
|---|---|
| wrkflw agreed with GitHub on 2 of 6 commits | false passes and false failures |
| `gate` on a feature branch or detached HEAD ran 0 workflows and passed | push "verified" with nothing checked |
| Running from a git worktree lost `.git` | every git step failed, masking real failures |
| Docker Desktop's 8 GB VM killed the linker | a failure GitHub's 16 GB runner never sees |
| itsdangerous planned 6 matrix legs, GitHub ran 7 | `include` semantics differed |
| `runs-on: ${{ matrix.os \|\| 'ubuntu-latest' }}` | windows and macOS legs were not flagged as unverified |
| Workflows without `name:` failed to parse | |
| Reused jobs looked like ordinary passes | |
| Digests had colour codes, `thiserror` as an error line, duplicated legs and a canned cargo hint | |

## What changes

- **Verdicts.** `run_finished` and `gate` gain `verdict`: `verified`, `partial`, or `nothing_checked`. The gate's `passed` is false when nothing ran. It still exits 0 then, so pushes that no CI covers aren't blocked.
- **Gate event fallback.** Without `--event`, a workflow a push doesn't fire is checked as a `pull_request` into the default branch. Each workflow entry says which `event` and `base_branch` it was checked as.
- **Matrix `include`** follows GitHub's documented rules. The documented example and itsdangerous are now tests.
- **`runs-on` expressions** that read only `matrix` are evaluated per leg.
- **Worktrees** get a real `.git` directory, mirrored from the common dir, on the right branch.
- **Memory.** A Docker or Podman VM under 14 GB triggers a warning and a limit of one job per 4 GB. `WRKFLW_MAX_PARALLEL_JOBS` overrides the limit. The digest names an `out_of_memory` cause.
- **Digest quality.** ANSI codes are stripped and error lines match whole words, skipping zero counts. Folded legs go under `also_failed_in`. The cargo hint is removed.
- **`reused`** is now set on `job_finished` and on `run_finished.jobs`.
- **New `wrkflw compare <run id|url>`.** It runs a finished GitHub run locally and lists per-job agreement, with notes on why results may differ.
- **`scripts/conformance/plan_corpus.sh`** plans the latest run of each workflow in 20 public repos and compares job counts. It needs `gh` and `jq`, and runs nothing.
- **Parser and schema gaps found by that corpus:**
  - a strategy without a matrix (psf/requests)
  - top-level `cache-mode`, `environment.deployment` and expression `timeout-minutes` (ruff)
  - the `code-quality` permission (clap)
  - empty env values (ripgrep)

Breaking changes are listed in `BREAKING_CHANGES.md`.

## Verified

- `cargo test --workspace --all-features` passes all 1,621 tests. `clippy -D warnings`, `fmt --check` and `check --no-default-features` are clean.
- **Compare**, on a commit where GitHub passed: all jobs agree. On a commit where GitHub's Ubuntu build failed: one disagreement, noted as "ran as macOS locally".
- **Gate**, on a feature branch: CI was checked as a pull request into main, with verdict `partial`. Before this change it ran nothing and passed.
- **Worktree run:** succeeds.
- **Docker build-only run on an 8 GB VM:** the memory warning is shown, the digest cause is `out_of_memory`, and the other legs are folded into `also_failed_in`.
- **Plan corpus:**
  - Every comparable workflow matches GitHub's job count.
  - The six workflows wrkflw could not parse now plan.
  - Workflows are marked n/a when GitHub skipped or cancelled jobs, when they call other workflows, or when no job ran.

## Not in this PR

- A scheduled CI job that runs the corpus or a self-compare. The script is documented, not automated.
- macOS and Windows jobs still run as Linux or as the host OS. They are reported as `partial`, not emulated.
